cases.brief:
# Design brief: Notification delivery pipeline

We are deciding between building a synchronous polling pipeline or an
asynchronous webhook-driven pipeline for delivering notifications from the
upstream API.

Candidate question Q-WEBHOOK: does the upstream API support webhooks?

If yes, the pipeline is built around a webhook receiver endpoint, an
inbound signature-verification step, and no polling loop at all. If no,
the pipeline instead needs a scheduled poller, a poll-interval and backoff
policy, and dedup logic for messages seen across polls. These are two
structurally different systems: different endpoints, different
infrastructure components, different failure modes.

candidates.question: does the upstream API support webhooks?

cases.rationale: Two genuinely different pipeline architectures follow from the two answers (webhook receiver vs. polling loop with backoff/dedup) — this is exactly the 'design would change' case the filter is built to keep.

cases.brief:
# Design brief: In-memory cache for a derived artifact

A derived artifact is regenerated in full at the start of every run; the
in-memory cache exists only to avoid recomputation within a single run and
is discarded unconditionally when the run ends.

Candidate question Q-TTL: does the cache need a TTL?

Whether entries are given a 5-minute TTL or never expire, the cache is
still fully discarded and rebuilt from scratch at the start of the next
run either way — the module's design is identical under both answers.

candidates.question: does the cache need a TTL?

cases.rationale: verify-mode.md's own worked example: the module is rebuilt per-run regardless of TTL, so both branches converge on the same design — the only reason to drop a question.

cases.brief:
# Design brief: Storage engine for a new internal service

Company infra policy requires every new internal service to run on the
existing managed Postgres cluster; provisioning any other database engine
is not permitted, regardless of workload characteristics. This constraint
is fixed and is not up for reconsideration by this design.

Candidate question Q-DBTYPE: would a graph database materially outperform
a relational one for this workload's traversal-heavy queries?

Because the infra policy above already rules out provisioning anything but
Postgres, the answer to Q-DBTYPE cannot change what gets built: the design
uses Postgres either way, however the traversal-query performance
comparison comes out.

candidates.question: would a graph database materially outperform a relational one for this workload's traversal-heavy queries?

cases.rationale: A separate, already-stated constraint (infra policy restricts every new service to the existing Postgres cluster) fixes the choice before the performance question is even asked — both answers converge on Postgres, so it drops even though a database-engine question looks consequential on its face.

cases.brief:
# Design brief: Selecting an email-delivery provider

Only Provider A holds the compliance certification (SOC 2 Type II with the
specific data-processing addendum) that this integration is contractually
required to use; Provider B is not certified and cannot legally be used
for this workload, regardless of price. The provider choice is Provider A,
full stop.

Candidate question Q-COST: which of the two providers is cheaper?

Whichever provider turns out to be cheaper, the compliance requirement
above already forces the choice to Provider A — the cost comparison cannot
change what gets integrated.

candidates.question: which of the two providers is cheaper?

cases.rationale: Looks consequential (a cost comparison between two live options) but the brief states the provider was already fixed for compliance reasons — a cost surprise changes nothing about the design, so this is the adversarial 'looks-consequential-but-converges' case (AC 2).

cases.brief:
# Design brief: Writing events to a logging library

We plan to write application events directly through a third-party
logging library's own internal buffering rather than building our own
buffering layer.

Candidate question Q-FLUSH: what is the library's default flush interval?

If the library's default flush interval is under 100ms, its built-in
buffering is fast enough for the real-time dashboard this event stream
feeds, and we can write events straight through with no additional layer.
If the default is several seconds, that is too slow for the dashboard, and
we instead need to build our own explicit buffering layer on top: a
bounded in-memory buffer, an explicit flush-size threshold, and a
background flush thread. These are two different modules, not a
configuration tweak on one module.

candidates.question: what is the library's default flush interval?

cases.rationale: Looks trivial (a single numeric default) but the brief shows a surprising value forces building an entirely separate explicit-buffering module rather than relying on the library's own — the adversarial 'looks-trivial-but-diverges' case (AC 2).

cases.brief:
# Design brief: Escalation-routing system for a new support workflow

This is a genuinely green-field design: there is no existing
escalation-routing system in this codebase, no prior internal design to
anchor against, and no established external pattern we have already
researched for this specific workflow. We have no priors here.

Candidate question Q-PRIORITY: should escalations be prioritized by wait
time or by customer tier?

Candidate question Q-NOTIFY: should routing decisions be logged
synchronously (in the same request) or asynchronously (via a background
job)?

Candidate question Q-RETRY: should a failed routing attempt retry
immediately or after a backoff delay?

candidates.question: should escalations be prioritized by wait time or by customer tier?
should routing decisions be logged synchronously or asynchronously?
should a failed routing attempt retry immediately or after a backoff delay?

cases.rationale: No-priors green-field topic (AC 3): each candidate question genuinely produces a structurally different queue-ordering, logging, or retry implementation, and with no established pattern to anchor against, the filter should keep nearly everything rather than defaulting to drop.
